title: Domestic workers: homes are workplaces too
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Millions work in homes without a central law of their own. What ILO C189, the Labour Codes, the Supreme Court and State laws say, and what workers and households can do.
body:
Domestic workers cook, clean, wash and care for children and the elderly in other people's homes. Their work lets millions of others go to offices, factories and courts every morning. Yet the law has been slow to treat a home as a workplace. This post looks at what international standards say, what protections exist in India today, where the gaps are, and what unions and residents' associations can do.

## An international standard that India has not ratified

In 2011 the International Labour Organization adopted the **Domestic Workers Convention (No. 189)**, the first international treaty to say plainly that domestic workers are workers and are entitled to the same basic labour rights as others. According to the ILO, those rights include reasonable hours of work, a weekly rest of at least 24 consecutive hours, a limit on payment in kind, clear information on the terms and conditions of employment, and respect for freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Convention also asks for special care for workers who face extra risks because of their young age, nationality or because they live in the employer's home.

The ILO estimated, on the basis of national surveys and censuses in 117 countries, that about 53 million people do domestic work worldwide, and noted that the true figure could be as high as 100 million because the work is so often hidden and unregistered. About 83 percent are women or girls, and many are migrants. Uruguay was the first country to ratify the Convention, in June 2012. India is not among the countries that have ratified it; a press report on a Bengaluru domestic workers' union campaign put the number of ratifying countries at 36 when it urged the Centre to ratify.

## How many domestic workers are there in India?

Nobody knows precisely. One policy summary notes that official statistics count about 4.75 million domestic workers, roughly three million of them women, while ILO and other estimates run much higher, with figures between 20 and 80 million quoted. The wide gap is itself the finding. Where work happens inside private homes, without a written contract, without a registered employer and often through informal placement agents, it is difficult to count and still harder to inspect. The same summary reports that about 81 percent of domestic workers are in informal employment and that, in a 2016 Bengaluru survey, only 2 percent had written contracts.

## What protections exist today

India has no single central law dedicated to domestic workers. Protection comes from a patchwork:

- **Minimum wages.** The Code on Wages, 2019 provides for minimum wages for all workers rather than only those in scheduled employments, according to the Labour Ministry's summary of the four Labour Codes brought into effect on 21 November 2025. In practice, an earlier summary found only about ten States had brought domestic work under their minimum-wage notifications, and enforcement was weak even there.
- **State laws and boards.** Tamil Nadu recognised domestic workers under a manual labour law as far back as 1999, Maharashtra set up a Domestic Workers Welfare Board under a 2008 Act, and Kerala introduced a Domestic Workers (Regulation and Welfare) Bill in 2021, as the Supreme Court itself noted.
- **Sexual harassment law.** The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 covers informal-sector women, including domestic workers. Where an employer has fewer than ten employees, complaints go to a Local Committee that the district officer is required to set up. Human Rights Watch reported in 2020 that many districts had not formed these committees and that workers often did not know they existed.
- **Social security.** The Code on Social Security treats domestic workers as unorganised workers who can be brought under notified welfare schemes. The Labour Codes also make appointment letters mandatory for all workers.
- **e-Shram.** The national database of unorganised workers, launched on 26 August 2021, had more than 30.98 crore registrations by August 2025, according to a Ministry reply in Parliament. Registration gives a Universal Account Number and, as the Ministry describes, links workers to schemes such as accident insurance and health cover.

## What the Supreme Court said, and what followed

In January 2025, in a case concerning the alleged wrongful confinement of a domestic worker, the Supreme Court noted that there is no pan-India law protecting domestic workers. The Court observed that most come from marginalised communities and often take up the work out of financial need, and it asked the Union Government to have the Labour Ministry, along with the Ministries of Social Justice, Women and Child Development and Law, constitute an expert committee to examine whether a legal framework for domestic workers is desirable.

According to a January 2026 report in *Down To Earth*, the committee's report, prepared in July 2025, concluded that a separate law is not needed because domestic workers are already covered by the four Labour Codes. Grassroots organisations disagreed. One researcher quoted in the report said the Codes are built around formal employer-employee relationships and the report did not explain how coverage would work in practice for a woman who works in five homes for a few hours each. This is the heart of the matter: a law can include domestic workers on paper, yet fail them if no one registers the employer, issues a slip, inspects the home or hears a complaint.

## The problems workers report

- **No contract, no fixed hours, no weekly off.** The ILO has noted that live-in workers in some countries work more than 60 hours a week, are expected to be on call at all hours, and may lack uninterrupted sleep. It has suggested an "11/24" rule: eleven consecutive hours of daily rest and 24 hours of weekly rest as a minimum starting point.
- **Unpaid wages and abrupt dismissal.** A study of Kochi, Delhi and Mumbai found that 57 percent of domestic workers surveyed were dismissed without compensation during the COVID-19 lockdown.
- **Harassment and abuse**, including by placement agencies, and restricted movement for live-in workers.
- **No maternity benefit, health cover or pension**, because there is often no identifiable establishment to contribute to such schemes.
- **Low and task-based pay.** Wages are often fixed per task rather than per hour, which hides the real length of the working day.

## What is asked

Unions across the spectrum have long asked for a **national law or at least a national policy** that provides for a minimum wage, weekly rest, registration of workers and employers, regulation of placement agencies and a grievance system that a worker can actually reach. A Draft National Policy on Domestic Workers prepared in 2019 proposed several of these but, according to one summary, has not been implemented. Others ask that India ratify Convention 189, as a statement that domestic work is real work.

BMS has consistently asked that labour laws be applied to all workers without exclusion, and its 2026 national conference at Puri placed that demand at the head of its resolutions. For domestic workers this means, first, a clear statutory duty on employers; second, simple registration and a portable benefit account through e-Shram; and third, an accessible dispute forum close to where the worker lives.

## What residents and employers can do now

Law will take time. Meanwhile, much can be done by those who employ domestic help:

1. Agree on a **fair wage and a weekly off** and write it down, even on a simple sheet signed by both sides.
2. Pay on time, give a leave allowance, and do not deduct for breakage without discussion.
3. Help the worker register on **e-Shram** and, where available, on the State welfare board.
4. In apartment complexes, let the **resident welfare association** agree a common wage band, working hours and a code of conduct for all residents.
5. Never accept the confinement of a worker, withholding of identity papers or wages, or the employment of children. These are offences, not household customs.

Domestic work is the work that makes other work possible. A society that depends on it every day owes it a contract, a wage and a day of rest.
